'''''Encephalartos lebomboensis''''' is a species of [[cycad]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Zamiaceae]]. Native to the [[Lebombo Mountains]] of [[South Africa]], the species was first described in 1949 by the South African botanist [[Inez Clare Verdoorn|Inez Verdoorn]].<ref name=Reynolds>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/encephlebomb.htm |title=''Encephalartos lebomboensis'' |author=Yvonne Reynolds |date=April 2003 |publisher=South Africa National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=2013-02-20 |archive-date=2013-05-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526180124/http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantefg/encephlebomb.htm }}</ref> It is commonly known as the '''Lebombo cycad''', although the name is also used for ''[[Encephalartos senticosus]]'' which also occurs in the same locality.<ref name="ARKive">{{cite web|url=http://www.arkive.org/lebombo-cycad/encephalartos-senticosus/|title=Lebombo cycad (''Encephalartos senticosus'')|publisher=ARKive|access-date=December 10, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215063647/http://www.arkive.org/lebombo-cycad/encephalartos-senticosus/|archive-date=2013-12-15}}</ref>

==Description==
''Encephalartos lebomboensis'' has a trunk that is up to {{convert|4|m}} tall and {{convert|30|cm}} thick; though the trunk is usually unbranched, suckers often form at the base and it sometimes bears offsets part way up. Often a number of stems form a clump. The crown of pinnate leaves are stiff, each having a mid to dark green glossy upper surface and paler under side. They are densely hairy at first but soon become hairless. They are {{convert|100|to|150|cm|in|-1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|20|to|27|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide, straight or slightly arched, either flat or with a slight keel. The leaflets are lanceolate and have serrated edges. They are up to {{convert|18|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide, held at right angles to the [[rachis]] and slightly overlapping. Near the base of the leaves, the leaflets are reduced to prickles.<ref name=Reynolds/><ref name=CSSA>{{cite web |url=http://www.cycadsociety.org/lebomboensis/lebomboensis.html |title=''Encephalartos lebomboensis'' Verdoorn |year=2002 |publisher=The Cycad Society of South Africa |access-date=2013-02-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130225124946/http://www.cycadsociety.org/lebomboensis/lebomboensis.html |archive-date=2013-02-25 }}</ref>

''E. lebomboensis'' is a [[Dioecy|dioecious]] species, that is, with separate male and female plants. Male specimens have one, or rarely two, short-stalked yellowish-orange cylindrical cones {{convert|40|to|45|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|12|to|15|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide. Female specimens have one or rarely two barrel-shaped cones, {{convert|40|to|45|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|25|to|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide, which are yellowish-green in colour. The seed coats are glossy red.<ref name=Reynolds/>

==Distribution==
''Encephalartos lebomboensis'' has two separate populations, one in the vicinity of [[Mananga]] in [[Mpumalanga]] province in South Africa and a southern population centred on [[Piet Retief, Mpumalanga|Piet Retief]]ion in the upper [[Pongola River|Pongola River Valley]]. It is a very rare and endangered species and grows in sunny positions on cliffs and steep, rocky slopes among sparse vegetation. This region has hot, fairly wet summers and cool, dry winters with frequent mists.<ref name=Reynolds/><ref name=CSSA/> It is also native to [[Mozambique]] and [[Eswatini]].<ref name="WCSP_385205">{{cite web |title=''Encephalartos lebomboensis''|work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=https://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=385205 |access-date=2015-08-11}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The form of this cycad found in the southern locality differs in certain characteristics from that growing in its northern enclave and it is considered to be a separate species, ''[[Encephalartos senticosus]]''. In 1996 ''E. senticosus'' was split from ''E. lebomboensis''.<ref>Threatened Plant Conservation Unit (2004) A Management Plan For Cycads In Kwazulu-Natal. Biodiversity Conservation Advice Division, Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, Kwazulu-Natal, South Africa. Available at: 
http://www.cycadsg.org/pages/publications.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120508152309/http://www.cycadsg.org/pages/publications.htm |date=2012-05-08 }}</ref><ref>The Cycad Pages (January, 2010)</ref> The main differences between the two are in the number, size and form of the male and female cones.<ref name=Reynolds/>

==Status==
There are believed to be about 5,000 specimens of ''Encephalartos lebomboensis'' growing in the wild.<ref name="iucn status 11 November 2021" /> It is a popular species with plant collectors and the [[IUCN Red List of Threatened Species]] lists it as being "[[Endangered species|Endangered]]" because of its over-exploitation and the degradation of its habitat due to the encroachment of agricultural land. It is listed in [[CITES#Appendix I|Appendix I]] of the CITES Appendices.<ref name="iucn status 11 November 2021" /> It is widely available as a cultivated plant.<ref name=CSSA/>
